The first line uses reasoning to investigate the fault of *asmimāna* (the conceit "I am"). The next four lines, based on the sūtras and śāstras, reveal the loss caused by *asmimāna*.
The phrase "the vessel [of pride] looks upward" clarifies the merit of contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā*). "Looking down upon beings" reveals the characteristics of pride regarding self and others;
because one stubbornly clings to them and refuses to accept wholesome dharmas, it is called "fourfold delusion. Being both deluded and obscured, one does not know where craving resides. Therefore...

It is said: "concealing" (*paryavasthāna*). Regarding the "covered vessel," this refers to the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* cited previously. As for the mention of the "sūtra," since that treatise cites the Buddha’s words, it takes the concealment of the mind by false speech as the "covered vessel.
Here, however, taking the high elevation of the mountain of pride as the "covered vessel" is a case of following the literal phrasing rather than the underlying intent.
"Harboring" refers to the aforementioned views and attachments; these can cause one to firmly cling to self and others, which is [the obstruction to] goodness.
It is said that [the number] cannot be eight. Regarding the treatise (*śāstra*) that elucidates the meaning of "taking in smoke," the term "treatise" refers to the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*.
Its second fascicle states: A cowherd asked the Buddha, "By the accomplishment of how many factors can a herd of cattle be made to multiply?
By the non-accomplishment of how many factors does a herd of cattle fail to increase and fail to attain peace? The Buddha replied, "There are eleven factors, O cowherd."

One is able to cause the herd of cattle to multiply. This refers to knowing the color, knowing the marks, knowing how to groom them, knowing how to treat sores, knowing how to produce smoke [as a signal], knowing the good paths, knowing the places suitable for cattle, knowing the good fords, knowing the safe locations, knowing when to withhold milk, and knowing how to care for the owner of the cattle or the cowherd.
If a cowherd knows these eleven dharmas and so forth, they are explained in their respective order. Regarding the first...
In five-character verse: How does one know how to produce smoke? To ward off mosquitoes and gadflies. When a cow sees smoke from afar, it comes toward the house.

The bhikṣu is also like this: speaking according to what he has heard, he wards off the mosquitoes and gadflies of the fetters (saṃyojana) by using the smoke of the Dharma to lead sentient beings into the house of the true mark of non-self and emptiness. Now, I shall borrow the meaning from the treatises to explain the intent.
This means that preaching the Dharma is like smoke. If sentient beings inhale the smoke of the Dharma, it leads them to the house of emptiness, the true mark of non-self.
Once they no longer harbor attachments, the mosquitoes and gadflies of craving and affection will flee and hide away. The vessel being tilted upward is a metaphor for receiving wholesome dharmas;
once these wholesome dharmas have entered, the root of pride will surely be eliminated. "There is nothing one does not submit to through reflection" is from the *Mao Shi*; it says: "From oneself..."
From the east to the west, from the south to the north, there are none who do not submit without thought. When the chamber collapses, there is no self; the house is empty.

The mosquitoes and gadflies of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) are dispersed by the smoke of preaching the Dharma. Thereafter, the fire of wisdom blazes forth, illuminating all delusions so that they become like the great void.
Views, cravings, and afflictions are extinguished of their own accord without being eliminated. Therefore it is said: "The body finds no place to rest. Furthermore, pride has no [ground].
Because they receive the Dharma, they are likened to an overturned vessel. Because I harbor attachments, I am likened to one inhaling smoke.

To turn one's back on this and to deviate from it constitutes the first [point]. This applies equally to ordinary beings and sages. "Attaining through emotional circumstances" refers to what is practiced by oneself; "being appropriate for transformation" refers to conforming to the Buddha’s words.
These two together point to the two dharmas of pride and the self.

Regarding the section on "Manifesting Faults by Way of Time": As for the terms *rán* (then) and *zé* (so), the *Mao Shī Zhèngyì* (Correct Meaning of the Mao Commentary on the Classic of Poetry) states:

"*Rán*" refers to what was said above; "*zé*" refers to what follows below. This is due to the momentum of what precedes giving rise to what succeeds. The "time of the True Dharma" (*saddharma*) refers to the era of the Buddha’s lifetime; the "final age of the Semblance Dharma" (*pratirūpaka-dharma*) refers to the degenerate times.
[The passage] "retreat from the seat" is taken from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. It says: "In that assembly there were bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas..."
The laywoman Sē together with five thousand others rose from their seats, paid homage to the Buddha, and withdrew.
This was because the Tathāgata desired to reveal to sentient beings the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, leading them to awaken and enter therein.

Yet those of overweening pride, who had not attained yet claimed to have attained, and who had not realized yet claimed to have realized, did not understand these skillful means; they remained trapped in the "transformed city," suppressing their own spiritual potential and failing to reflect.
The reason for this treasure-seal is that those who are deluded fail to realize that their own nature is fundamentally that of a Buddha; this refers to those followers who cling to existence.

It is like the land of those who disregard their lives—just as there are certain people in the world today who engage in lofty talk and grand discourse, yet devote themselves only to intellectual disputation and neglect diligent cultivation.
They claim, "I have cut off the flow of all phenomena; there is no need for cultivation or realization," knowing only how to study.

[They] speak [thus], disregarding their own conduct. Indulging in dissipation and licentiousness, they lack any restraint; thus they hold themselves in low esteem, failing to realize that the body is the vessel for cultivating the Way.
Now, with afflictions (*kleśa*) not yet severed and the fruit of the Path (*mārgaphala*) not yet realized, they recklessly destroy and discard themselves.
Is this not to treat life lightly? These are merely those who cling to emptiness (*śūnyatā*). "Abundant" (*fēng*) means much. The *Yèshù* (Outline of Karma) says: "One must deeply..."
Regarding measurement: what kind of person is it that can subsequently attain self-elevation and transcend the world? This corresponds to what the Confucians say:

"If one cannot find a person of the Middle Way with whom to associate, one must resort to the *kuang* (the impetuous) and the *xuan* (the cautious). The *kuang* person strives for advancement; the *xuan* person refrains from certain actions.
Being mired in delusion for long kalpas is the *xuan* person’s "refraining from certain actions"; those who disregard their own lives are the *kuang* person.
This is progress. Yet both have been unable to practice the simultaneous integration of emptiness and existence or to move freely between the ultimate and the conventional;
they merely know to cling to one side and are unable to undergo the three reversals.

Within the section on lamentation: first, the teaching instructs one to contemplate and thoroughly understand that both body and mind are illusory. The following passage from the sutra provides scriptural proof for this.
What follows is the concluding lamentation. Regarding the point that "the body belongs to external conditions":

because it is produced by one's parents, or alternatively, because it is induced as a retribution by past causes and conditions, it is said to depend on external conditions. Regarding "darkly lacking all knowledge": before birth, one was unaware.
Because of the place from which one comes. Ordinary people below have not yet awakened; only by attaining the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*) can one know where one has come from.

A monk from Shu named Kang Lang composed a verse: Before the Lord of Heaven gave birth to me, In the darkness, I knew nothing at all. Suddenly the Lord of Heaven gave birth to me— Having given birth to me, what was it for?
No clothes leave me cold; no food leaves me hungry. Return me back to you, O Lord of Heaven! Return!

"When I was not yet born, the spirit belonged to delusion and karma. Here, "delusion" refers to the path of afflictions (*kleśa-mārga*), and "karma" refers to the path of action (*karma-mārga*); both belong to the mind.
This is further investigated as the worldly affairs of beginningless time, together with the aforementioned reward body (*vipākakāya*), forming the three paths.

One revolves in this cycle without awakening. The scripture referred to is the *Zuòchán sānmèijīng* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of Seated Meditation). The current excerpt is disorganized; the full text states:
"Today one engages in this task; tomorrow one undertakes that matter. Delighting in them and failing to contemplate suffering, one does not perceive the arrival of the thief of death.
It is further said: "Who can know the time of death, or by which path one shall go? It is like a lamp in the wind; its moment of extinction is unknown," and so forth.
Among the three types of *kandhu*, *kaṇḍu* refers to the pea (*māṣa*). *Kaṇḍu* means interference; *cintā* (rendered here as *lù*) means mental anxiety. This is a metaphor.

The people of the world revolve upon the wheel of the three paths. If they lack the nourishment of roots of goodness, even when they encounter virtuous words, they are unwilling to believe or accept them;
they may be called withered sentient beings, further unable to receive the waters of meditative concentration and wisdom.
These words originate from the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, which says: "For example, when peas are dry, a awl cannot pierce them; likewise, the hard crust of afflictions is the same."

Furthermore, in the first section of the comparative analysis of these and other such [passages], regarding the three types of "equal wisdom" (*samatājñāna*), the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "All sentient beings possess equal wisdom with respect to three things:
namely, sexual desire, food and drink, and fear. This refers to the fact that although humans and animals differ in their endowments...
They are different, yet their wisdom is of one kind; therefore, it is called "equal wisdom" (*sāmaññā-ñāṇa*). I am currently unable to cultivate the Path, and my wisdom is the same as theirs;
hence it is said, "My wisdom is equal to that of oxen and sheep. Nevertheless, among humans there exists the supramundane Noble Path and a certain kind of wisdom that oxen and sheep lack;
therefore, it is said they are "not of the same class. "Class" (*lun*) means equality. This is an exegesis from the perspective of the inferior human realm. [End of section].
The Way is beyond comparison. The first two lines clarify that human nature ought to practice [the Way]; if one does not do so now, one is no different from beasts.

Regarding the "conditions of the Way," the Great Master said: "Only this human path has pleasure that is inferior and suffering that is light; the higher realms have suffering that is slight, while the lower destinies possess powerful consciousness."
The power of mindfulness can cultivate the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*). This means that the human body as a vessel is the necessary condition for cultivating the path.

Regarding those who are no different from beasts, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Though the six sense faculties are complete and their intellectual discernment is clear and sharp, if one does not seek the Dharma of the Path, one receives in vain a body endowed with wisdom.
Even birds and beasts know sensual pleasure and indulge in it at will, yet they do not know the proper direction."

One should instead cultivate wholesome deeds for the sake of the Path. Having already obtained a human body, if one merely indulges in self-indulgence and does not know how to practice the Path, how is this different from those [other beings]?
Confucianists also say: "If a person lacks ritual propriety (*li*), though they have no worries, they are like birds.
Why do people not cultivate the Path and ritual propriety? Both Confucianism and Buddhism compare such individuals to the same as birds and beasts. The following two lines clarify this.

Beasts are unable to practice the path of a single wisdom that leads beyond [samsara]. Because the retribution for their afflictions and defilements is heavy, they constantly undergo suffering and distress;
since they cannot even save themselves, what leisure do they have to cultivate the supramundane holy path? Therefore, it is said that this is not what they hear.

Next, regarding the three sections on the exhortation to practice: first is the exhortation to realize the essence and carry out the observance; this is followed by the clarification of the benefits obtained by body and mind.

The passage beginning with "rat" (mouse) clarifies the timing for attaining mastery over the teachings and contemplations. Within the first section, the initial four lines concern knowing the excellence of retribution and initiating cultivation.

"Form" (*xing*) refers to the physical body. "Light and pure" (*qingqing*) means it is not the retribution of the three miserable realms. When the faculties of consciousness are activated, one is no longer muddled or obscured. [The term] "faculties" (*ji*)...

This refers to the agility and sharpness of the mental faculty. It is like the meaning of a king attending to ten thousand affairs daily: as soon as he acts, everything moves forward without confusion.

This is precisely the exhaustion of the suffering of birth and the unraveling of the accumulation of the net of delusions. Thus, the following clarifies that the Triple Gem is the object of cultivation.
The preceding two lines refer to the body taking refuge in the sacred image; "dust-accumulation" refers to the dust of the four great elements, which is merely provisional.
"Combined and gathered together" refers to what is stated in the following passage: "Reflecting carefully on the aggregation of forms, one sees only a mass of sensory objects.

The latter two lines concern the removal of the causes of mental delusion; prior to taking refuge in the Triple Gem, one is bound by the shackles of afflictions (*kleśa*), and thus one provisionally adopts a renewed mind through taking refuge and paying homage.
It is for the purpose of sweeping away [defilements] that it is so called. This, then, is the cultivation of the path of prostration, which realizes the extinction of afflictions.
To obtain benefit within the inner mind is what is meant by "the mind. That which distinguishes [humans] from oxen and sheep is due to the single kind of clear wisdom of the path of transcendence;
by taking refuge in and honoring the Triple Gem, one obtains benefit within the mental continuum. As for "carving to form a vessel," this refers to the physical vessel [of the body].
This refers to attaining benefit therein. "Carving" corresponds to wood above; "engraving" corresponds to stone above.

Among the three [categories], the four lines of the superior section arise from understanding the terminology and scriptural texts, whereby one realizes that body and mind should take refuge in the Triple Gem. Other celestial deities are not objects of refuge at all.
The term "name" (名) is an inversion of the word order; it should properly read "to lead by name" (引名言). Furthermore, this serves as an exhortation for the subsequent contemplation and self-urging.
"Zi" (dregs) refers to turbidity. The "four mountains" refer to birth, old age, sickness, and death. The meaning is this:

since one already dwells amidst the five turbidities and is further pressed by the four mountains, how could one continue to endure with complacency the affairs practiced in the world, remaining addicted to them and mired in ignorance without attaining realization?
Regarding the establishment of the teaching and the manifestation of its benefits, in the first section, the first two phrases clarify that the Great Sage discerns the capacities of sentient beings.
The character "tong" (通) is an error; the ancient text reads "shi" (適), meaning "timely transformation. "Tao" (陶) means to refine or mold, and "you" (誘) means to lead or entice;
this refers to the Tathāgata’s skillful means and his intention to descend into the world. The following four phrases establish the benefits of the Tathāgata’s establishment of deeds and words.
This is because sentient beings have been attached to heterodox views for a long time; therefore, the True Triple Gem was established to lead them away from such attachments.
"Turbid consciousness" refers to the heterodox mind, while "that to which one returns" refers to the True Triple Gem.

Since there were those who, before the Tathāgata appeared in the world, claimed to be masters of their own schools and likewise established their own "Triple Gems," it may be appropriate to refer here to the heterodox Triple Gems of Devadatta and others. The Four Seals.
This refers to the four seals (mudrā) of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*. In its fifty-eighth fascicle, it asks: "For what reason does the Buddha speak of the four seals? It answers:

"Because he wishes to explain the characteristics of the true Dharma of the Buddha. For the sake of future bhikṣus, so that they may clearly distinguish what is the word of the Buddha and what is not, he speaks of the seals.
One should know that those four seals are identical to the four broad [categories] of this root Vinaya."
It is so stated. Thus, that text says: "First, hearing from the Buddha; second, hearing before an elder among the Saṃgha;
third, hearing from many bhikṣus who know the Dharma; fourth, hearing from a single bhikṣu who knows the Dharma.

Regarding those who speak in such a manner, one should neither praise nor disparage them immediately. One should first verify them against the authoritative scriptures of the Tripiṭaka, and only then may one rely upon them.
By its application, one knows that our Buddha, the Most Holy One, deeply feared that sentient beings would become deluded and inverted, taking the false for the true and the right for the wrong;

therefore, he established this Dharma to distinguish between the false and the true. For those whose turbid consciousnesses cause them to wander in birth, when they receive the teachings with their own eyes, they are like guests who have descended from above.

The first two lines clarify his meritorious achievements, which are the benefits of his abiding maintenance [of the world]; the latter two lines manifest the retribution received, transmitted through the lineage.

“Tongyi” (Universal Benefit) refers to the ten thousand years; this is merely a general enumeration. The “four heavens” refer to Tuṣita. Since there are six heavens in the Desire Realm, Tuṣita corresponds to the fourth.
They are: first, the Heaven of the Four Great Kings; second, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; third, the Yāma Heaven; fourth, the Tuṣita Heaven;
fifth, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven; and sixth, the Paranirmitavaśavartin Heaven. “Cijing” (Sūtra of Compassion) refers to Maitreya.

The *Śūramgama-samādhi Sūtra* states: "After my parinirvāṇa, if the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings wish to be reborn in the fourth heaven, they should, for one day up to seven days, fix their mindfulness upon that heaven, uphold the Buddha’s prohibitions and precepts, and contemplate the ten wholesome deeds.
By dedicating these merits, they vow to be born before Maitreya Buddha. Since such a source exists, this is not a fabrication.
He establishes his argument; thus he says, "How could it be in vain?

In the first part of the next section, he explains the purpose for which the text was composed; following that, he reveals the literary structure of the work; and finally, he cites textual evidence from the Buddha’s teachings.
Within the first of these, the phrase "for the sake of beginners" indicates humility. The subsequent text provides a detailed and comprehensive exposition of the four kinds of *triple* [teachings].

The term "Treasure" (Bǎo) is used because the capacities of later students are dull. If one were to establish the matter for those of former excellence, it would mostly apply to those of sharp faculties;

hence it is said that its essence is not something to be anticipated prematurely. Furthermore, when the merit of the Three Jewels in saving the world is proclaimed and extended specifically to later students, those of former excellence have not yet been seen therein.
Moreover, the first two lines clarify the application to beginners, while the latter two lines speak of [the opposite].
I venture to present this to those who have already attained mastery. The second and third lines speak of its thoroughness; that is, it is a detailed instruction. "Ding-ning" (earnestly):
the *Zuozhuan* states, "To be earnest and repeated. "Pointing at the palm": this means pointing at an object held within the palm, signifying that it is easy to perceive.
This phrase originates from the *Lunyu*. "Pu" (to spread out) means to lay out or arrange. "Guan" (pronounced *luo-guo*) refers to examining the threads [of the matter]. To enumerate...
The "various" (zhǒng) refers to the four categories of the Three Jewels as a single essence. This is a provisional device established by the gate of teaching.
Regarding the phrase "the six groups" (*liù zhòng*), it is an error; it should read "the seven groups" (*qī zhòng*), namely the five groups of the ordained and the two groups of the laity.
Although they differ as monastics and laypeople, they are alike in taking the Buddha as their teacher and share a common aspiration. The words "only" (*wéi*) and below refer to the Great Master.
This is merely a matter of humility. Therefore, the following three phrases clarify the origin of the Buddha’s words;

that is, the characteristics of the Three Jewels across the four stages are established in accordance with the capacities and perceptions of sentient beings. To speak of "one essence" refers to the wondrous nature inherently possessed by all sentient beings.

Because delusion gives rise to consciousness, they are said to be of one substance. When cultivation reveals the principle of nature (dharmatā), one no longer remains in confusion; thus it is called the "substance of principle" (li-ti).

Once awakening is fulfilled and the realization of this principle is found to be non-illusory, one ought to respond to conditions and stimuli; hence there are manifested forms (nirmāṇa-lakṣaṇa) that accord with the world and undergo extinction.
The physical image remains in the world for sentient beings to take refuge in; as its source and flow are inexhaustible, there is the "abiding and maintaining" (zhuchi).

The four ranks follow one another in succession, hence they are arranged in order. If one follows the definitions of Xiachuan, there are three types; that which is called "abiding and maintaining" is identical to this.

Second, regarding the distinct characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*): it is said that the Buddha possesses the three bodies (*trikāya*)—the *dharmakāya*, *saṃbhogakāya*, and *nirmāṇakāya*. Within the *dharmakāya*, there are distinctions among the four stages of teaching, principle, practice, and fruition.

The Saṃgha is divided into eight classes and five ranks, with differences between the Great and Small Vehicles; hence they are called "distinct characteristics. Third, the single essence is also termed the "universal characteristic" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).

This means that within the nature of suchness (*tathatā*), that which has the meaning of awakening and realization is named the Buddha, and that which has the meaning of maintaining the norms is [named the Dharma].

That which is named "Dharma" possesses the meaning of harmony, and thus it is called the "Saṃgha. All sentient beings are endowed with these treasures; therefore, they are said to be of the same essence (*samavāya*).
As for the categories of the Three Jewels in other schools, which variously cite six kinds of the Three Jewels, those are not adopted here. Question:

Why is it that while the four kinds of the Three Jewels are fully explained in the section on "Aiding the Age," they are not explained in other sections? Answer: It is because the world [understands] them through their mutual manifestation.
These are not [mere] signs; they cannot move the human heart. Therefore, the four marks are enumerated to cause both monastics and laypeople to take refuge with faith.
Once faith has arisen, one may enter the three trainings. When the timing and conditions are met, the True Dharma can be practiced—is this not so? Question:

Regarding the four types mentioned here, how do they compare to the four types of the Three Jewels established in the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts)? Are they the same or different? Answer: The number four is no different. As for their establishment...

The meaning differs slightly. Regarding the abiding and sustaining of the manifested marks (*nirmāṇa-lakṣaṇa*), both [traditions] are the same. Regarding the single essence of the principle-body (*tattva-dharmakāya*), there is a difference in breadth and brevity.
This [text] provides a general discussion based on the Great and Small Vehicles, whereas that [text] provides a specific analysis based on its particular school.

In the brief explanation, because sentient beings and Buddhas are not different and delusion and enlightenment share the same source, the Buddha is itself the Dharma, and the Dharma is itself the Sangha; since they are understood to be entirely without distinction, it is called "Non-... (the *Avyūha*).

Second: Not only is this true of the Three Jewels; it is so for all phenomena (*dharma*). Thus, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "All sentient beings are suchness (*tathatā*). The *Ratnakaraṇḍa-sūtra* states:
"The Buddha-realm and the sentient-being realm are one realm; there is no separate realm. Nevertheless, one awakens to and realizes all phenomena.
Pervading all places, even within the five *ānantarya* (uninterrupted) offenses, there is liberation. This principle is self-evident: the phenomenal world is eternally abiding;
whether a Buddha appears does not benefit it, nor does the absence of a Buddha diminish it. To attain it is no cause for exultation; to lose it is no cause for dejection.

The principle is fundamentally complete. What is called the "fundamental consciousness" (*mūlavijñāna*) is the single mind alone within the three realms, and the sole reality among the myriad phenomena.

The single consciousness is inherently possessed by all sentient beings; it is not something acquired only now. In Sanskrit it is called *ālaya*; in this land [of China] it is translated as the "storehouse consciousness" (*ālayavijñāna*).
It is also termed the "indeterminate," the "ignorance," and the "latent tendency"—it is precisely the eighth consciousness. It is also sometimes called *ādāya*.
This is translated as "grasping and maintaining" (*ādāna*); these are merely differences in the translations by various masters.

For instance, the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha translates it as "non-perishing consciousness" (*amala-vijñāna*), taking the sense of abiding, maintaining, and not being lost. The Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang translates it as "containing and storing" (*ālaya-vijñāna*), taking the sense of containing, encompassing, and concealing within.
This means that it can store its own nature within all phenomena, and it can also store all phenomena within its own essence.
What is called the *ālaya* of sentient beings is the Tathāgata’s pure treasury; this is precisely the principle that the source of birth and Buddhahood is identical.

This is based on the *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages) which clarifies that the *ālayavijñāna* is the true, eternal, and pure consciousness. If one follows the *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃgraha), the eighth *ālayavijñāna* is a consciousness characterized by indeterminate ignorance and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
A ninth consciousness is established separately, named the "Pure Treasury" (*viśuddhagarbha*), distinguishing between delusion and awakening.

This is the treatise. Therefore, the present unity is established by taking the essence of delusion as the basis and approximating it to awakening; this too is its underlying principle. Furthermore, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "Briefly stated, there are three kinds of consciousness:
namely, the true consciousness (*tathatā-vijñāna*), the manifesting consciousness (*khyāti-vijñāna*), and the consciousness that discriminates phenomena (*vicitra-vastu-vijñāna*).
A verse says: "It is like a vast ocean wave, stirred up by a fierce wind; the great billows surge through the depths of the sea, never ceasing for a moment. (This metaphor clarifies the point.)

The ocean of the *ālayavijñāna* abides eternally (this is the *tathatā-vijñāna*). It is stirred by the winds of objective realms (this is the *pratibhāsa-vijñāna*). The various waves of consciousness surge and arise in succession (this is the *vijñapti-vijñāna*;

the above is the explanation in terms of Dharma). Furthermore, it is said: "That which is called the *ālayavijñāna* is named 'mind' (*citta*); that whose nature is deliberation is 'intellect' (*manas*);
and that which can discern the characteristics of all objects is therefore called 'consciousness' (*vijñāna*). Thus, these are the three characteristics of mind, intellect, and consciousness.
[This concludes] the separate section. Furthermore, the *Mahāvaipulya Tathāgatagarbha Sūtra* states: The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Vajramati:

"Suppose there were countless lotus flowers manifested by a Buddha that suddenly withered and decayed. Within these lotuses, immeasurable transformation Buddhas sat cross-legged, adorned with the primary and secondary marks, emitting great radiance.
When the multitude beheld this rarity, there was none who did not pay them reverence. It is thus."

"Good son, with my Buddha-eye I observe all sentient beings; within their greed, anger, ignorance, and all other afflictions, there exists the Tathāgata’s wisdom, the Tathāgata’s eye, and the Tathāgata’s body, sitting cross-legged, majestic and unmoving.
Good son, although all sentient beings are within the various realms of existence and amidst bodies of affliction, the Tathāgatagarbha is eternally undefiled."

The marks of virtue are fully perfected, no different from my own. By means of these various texts as evidence, one knows that the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna) is fully endowed with the Three Jewels;
thus, the designation of the "Three Jewels of One Substance" is not established in vain.

In the section clearly elucidating the inherent nature (*prakṛti-prativedha*), the first two lines clarify original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*), while the subsequent lines manifest non-enlightenment (*a-bodhi*).

Regarding the statement within original enlightenment that "the nature is pure like space," the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "Like empty space, it has no nature of its own; all paths of language are cut off," and so forth.
The *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* says: "The essence of the mind is free from thought. That which is free from thought is equal to the realm of empty space, such that there is nothing it does not pervade."
Pervasive throughout the dharma-realm, it has a single characteristic; this is the Tathāgata’s equal Dharma-body, which is designated as "original enlightenment" (*mūla-awakening*).
Because the essence of this mind is all-pervasive, it is called the "dharma-realm. Because it gives rise to all phenomena, it is called the "Mother of Buddhas.

Because it is free from all marks, it is called "prajñā," or "dharma-nature," "buddha-nature," "śīla," "the Middle Way," or "true reality"—these are merely provisional names for Perfect Enlightenment.

Although the various names such as *Śūraṅgama* and others differ, they are none other than designations for the essence of the compassionate mind. As the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* states: "Prajñā is a single dharma;
the Buddha establishes various names for it. This is precisely what is meant. Within the state of non-awakening, deluded thought is the path of affliction (*kleśa-mārga*);

following defilement is the path of karma (*karma-mārga*); and birth-and-death is the path of suffering (*duḥkha-mārga*). The circulation through these three paths is like a waterwheel drawing from a well.

There is no means by which one may attain liberation. Regarding the terms "receptacle" (*āśraya*) and "dust" (*rajas*), a sutra states: Cunda addressed the Buddha, saying that through his realization of the two characters "guest-dust" (*āgantuka-rajas*), he achieved the fruit [of Arhatship].
The World-Honored One explained that "not abiding" is called the receptacle, while "wavering and moving" is called dust, and so forth.

Regarding the scriptural citations: the sutra is the *Guan jing* (Sutra on Contemplating the Lands). Its full title is *The Sutra on All Dharmas Being Empty and Quiescent in Their Nature and Characteristics from the Beginningless Past to the Present*.

As for what are called "all dharmas," to speak of them collectively, they refer to the dharmas of the ten dharma-realms—namely, those of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and so forth, down to those of the hells.
Formerly, these were referred to as the dharmas of the mind, the dharmas of the Buddha, and the dharmas of sentient beings. Furthermore, they are categorized as mundane and supramundane.

Regarding worldly dharmas, it is not that this meaning does not exist; what was stated above still applies generally. Next is the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. The passages cited therein are all from the "Tathāgata-gotra" chapter:
the first line and the second line speak of original endowment (*prakṛti-stha*), while the subsequent two lines manifest accomplishment through cultivation (*samudānīta*).
As for those who are deluded as ordinary beings and enlightened as sages, the ancients said: "The deluded are deluded of themselves; the enlightened are enlightened of themselves. (1)

The nature is profoundly clear; it is utterly devoid of coming or going. This is illustrated by the analogy of the poor woman. The four lines beginning with "The nature is constant" conclude the two preceding analogies.
Here, "light" is a metaphor for the jewel, and "manifestation" is a metaphor for the treasury. Regarding the mention of the "poor woman," the Sūtra states:
"All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, yet it is constantly shrouded by immeasurable afflictions; therefore, sentient beings are unable to perceive it. It is like...
Within the house of a poor woman, there is a great store of pure gold, yet none of her family members, whether young or old, are aware of it.
At that time, there was a person of extraordinary ability who, being skilled in expedient means, immediately excavated the golden treasure from within that house.
Son of good family, I now universally reveal to all sentient beings that their Buddha-nature is likewise covered and obscured by various afflictions, just as in the case of that poor woman.
"Daughter, there is a treasury of pure gold that one cannot see," and so forth. Regarding the "seven-jeweled bead on the forehead":
the Sūtra says, for example, there was a great athlete in a royal household. Between his eyebrows was a diamond bead (*vajramaṇi*).
While he was contending in a wrestling match with another athlete, that athlete struck him with his head; the bead on his forehead immediately sank into his skin, and he did not perceive it at all.
He knew where the jewel was located; there was a sore at that spot. He immediately summoned a skilled physician, wishing to treat it himself.
When the physician arrived, he held up a mirror to reflect his face, and the jewel appeared clearly within the mirror. It continues:
"Because all sentient beings cannot draw near to virtuous friends (kalyāṇamitra), although they possess the Buddha-nature (buddhadhātu), none of them can see it. And so forth.
"Enveloped by greed, hatred, and delusion," and so forth. "A treasure covered by deep thickets" refers to the *tathāgatagarbha* existing within the nature of afflictions (*kleśa*).
"Flowing with various flavors" refers to wandering through the six realms and undergoing rebirth. However, the concluding section below clarifies that what is inherently present is never lost.
As the Sūtra says: "Good son, it is like a mountain of snow where there is a medicinal herb of a single flavor."
It is named *Rasāyana* (the "Taste of Bliss" [the *Jíjiè* commentary states: the essence of the taste is not itself bliss, but it can produce bliss in people]). It grows beneath dense thickets;
no one is able to see it, yet anyone who smells its fragrance immediately knows that this medicine must be at that spot.
In ages past, there was a Cakravartin King who, for the sake of this medicine, constructed bamboo tubes here and there throughout these snowy mountains to receive the medicine. This medicine...
When it has matured, it flows from the ground and collects in its original conduit; its flavor is truly authentic.
After the king has passed away, this medicine subsequently becomes sour, salty, sweet, bitter, pungent, or bland.

Thus, while it is of a single flavor, according to where it flows, there appear various differences. This medicine of a single flavor is the Tathāgatagarbha; its being within the deep thicket is a metaphor.

The abundance of afflictions is like a dense forest where this Dharma cannot be seen. The metaphor of "smelling the fragrance" represents initial awakening (*ādikṣānti*). The metaphor of the "Wheel-Turning King" represents wondrous awakening (*samyaksaṃbodhi*).

The phrase "receiving those who enter the tube with joy wherever they may be" is a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s skillful means (*upāya*) in receiving sentient beings and causing them to enter the nature of perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*).
"Its flavor is true" is a metaphor for the various Dharma gates established through skillful means, all of which—[lead to the ultimate].

This is the wondrous Dharma. After the wheel-turning king has passed away—this being a metaphor for the Buddha’s entry into parinirvāṇa—and since there are no longer skillful means, one consequently undergoes the cycle of rebirth within the six realms.
The six flavors, such as sour and salty, correspond to these six realms. That which is inherently stainless is a metaphor for the buddha-nature of sentient beings;

although it remains amidst the dense thickets of the six classes of ordinary beings, its supernormal powers, functions, and marks of physical excellence are no different from those of a Buddha in fruition.
Furthermore, the latter two lines summarize the three metaphors. "Radiance" refers to the jewel on the forehead within a treasure trove;
"purity" refers to exquisite medicinal herbs in a deep thicket. All of the above clarify that these are inherently possessed.

The section on "Cultivation and Accomplishment" consists of two parts. From the beginning up to the point where it says "cultivation reveals," it clarifies how the Buddhas of the past cultivated and revealed the principle of the inherent nature.

From there up to the point where it says "the ultimate stage," it clarifies that later worthies seek this with unceasing resolve. Within the first part, the initial four lines clarify revealing the cause through the fruit;
the subsequent four lines distinguish the cultivation of the cause and the realization of the fruit. If this is so, one does not fall into the view of emptiness regarding cause and fruit.

It is evident. To speak of "transformation of the basis" (āśraya-parāvṛtti) means that there is no realization apart from realization; one realizes one’s own original *dharmakāya*. It is not a manifestation apart from manifestation;
it manifests one's own originally inherent virtues. In this way, cultivation and nature are non-dual, and the living being and the Buddha are of one suchness.
Next, regarding the aspiration for the intermediate [stage]: it is intended that all in the future may emulate those who have attained the fruit and engage in cultivation.

This is a summary of the general meaning; the formal text is drawn from the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. It says: "For example, two people hear together that in another land there is a mountain of seven treasures, upon which is a clear spring.
Its water is sweet and delicious; anyone who can reach it will forever sever poverty by drinking its water."
"To increase one's lifespan by ten thousand years, the way is indeed remote and filled with many dangers and hardships. At that time, those two men both desired to go together.
One prepared various provisions for the journey, while the other went empty-handed, carrying nothing at all.

As they proceeded forward, they encountered a man on the road who was carrying much wealth and possessed the seven kinds of precious jewels in full. The two men stepped forward and asked him: "O Virtuous One..."
"Does that land truly have mountains made of the seven treasures? The man replied, "It is indeed so; it is not false. I have already obtained the treasures and drunk its waters.
My only concern is that the road is perilous, with many bandits, salty sands, and thorns; there is a lack of water and grass.
Of those who go, ten million may set out, but very few reach their destination. Having heard these words, one person immediately felt regret and immediately spoke thus:
He said, "The road is already so remote and the hardships manifold; of those who have gone, few have reached their destination. How then can I possibly arrive there?
Another person spoke again, saying, "There are those who have passed through; I too shall pass through.
If I succeed in reaching my goal, I shall obtain the precious jewels as I wish, along with delicious food and sweet water. If I do not reach it, I shall regard death as [my end]."
At that time, the two men—one regretted his return while the other pressed forward—reached that mountain.

There they obtained many precious treasures, drank the water as desired, and took much of their belongings with them back to their dwelling. There they supported their parents and provided for their kinsmen.
When the one who had regretted his return saw this, his heart grew hot again, thinking: "He has already gone and returned; what am I doing here?"

He stopped and immediately adorned himself to set out on the road, and so forth. The seven-jeweled mountain is a metaphor for *nirvāṇa*. The sweet water is a metaphor for the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).

The one person who regrets his decision is a metaphor for a bodhisattva who has just resolved to attain enlightenment but is indolent. The one person who proceeds is a metaphor for a bodhisattva who has long practiced with diligence.
The perilous path is a metaphor for birth and death (*saṃsāra*). The bandits are a metaphor for the four maras. The thorns are a metaphor for the afflictions (*kleśa*). There is no...

The metaphor of the aquatic plants illustrates the difficulty of encountering a virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) who does not practice skillful means (*upāya*). The person encountered on the middle path is a metaphor for the Buddha.

Next, regarding the exhortation based on the vehicles (*yāna*), there are three parts. First, from the beginning up to "coming to respond to the call," it clarifies that the former sages have already attained realization. From "I have arrived" below...
The phrase "all who come" reveals the aspiration of later worthies to seek [the truth] until they reach the final text.

From "contemplation" through "arising practice," the first three phrases clarify that the principle realized by the true bodies (*dharmakāya*) of all Buddhas is not distinct; the latter three phrases clarify that the intention of the response bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) to benefit sentient beings is without partiality.
This vehicle is without expedient means; thus one knows that the three vehicles are merely provisional establishments. This is because, within the One...

The Buddha Vehicle (*buddhayāna*). Because it is explained through the differentiation of three [vehicles], the Buddha Vehicle is the true Dharma and not a provisional means (*upāya*). This is because throughout the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, there is only the Single Vehicle Dharma (*ekayāna*).
Nevertheless, for the sake of the jewel, the provisional is bestowed; within the provisional there is the real. By opening up the provisional, the real is revealed;

the real is accomplished by relying upon the provisional. Thus, the provisional and the real are non-dual; therefore, it is said that this vehicle does not exist. "The cage" refers to the tethering of a dog.

The implements for sentient beings are as follows: those made of wood are called *fán* (enclosures), and those made of bamboo are called *lóng* (cages). The *Erya* states: "The *fán* is the same as the *lóng*. It seems "bèiyí" should be read as "fǔyí"; I suspect a transmission error.

"Fùgǎn" (responding to resonance) means that the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) arises through great compassion of the same essence (*sahaja-mahākaruṇā*), in order to respond to the needs of living beings;

this is precisely its benevolent virtue. Because the Buddha’s single-vehicle nature (*ekayāna-gotra*) is manifested, he is able to respond; thus, the principle is inherently complete within all sentient beings.

Because of the One Vehicle, one is able to attain [enlightenment]. The two lines following "I" (in the verse) reveal that the birth [of sentient beings] and the Buddha are of one suchness (*tathatā*).

The two lines following "He" (the Buddha) clarify that the Buddha was first awakened; the two lines following "I" lament that I have already sunk into delusion. "Hesitating" (*pan-huan*) means being unable to advance in virtue or cultivate one's practice.
As the *Zhou Yi*, Hexagram Zhun, states: "The first nine: hesitating. The commentary notes: "Being at the beginning of Zhun, movement gives rise to doubt."
One cannot advance; therefore, it is called "hesitating" (*pánhuán*). First, contemplate that clear mindfulness and awakening must be cultivated.
If one does not cultivate them now, there will be no refuge in future lives. What is the basis for this? "Basis" (*jù*) means the same as "refuge" (*tuò*); it also means "reliance."

Within the dharmas cultivated through the Threefold Knowledge (*traividyā*), the first part generally clarifies the Three Trainings (*triśikṣā*). The first two lines clarify the subduing and extinguishing of afflictions and karma; the latter two lines refer to the refinement of the three bodies (*trikāya*).

"Inheriting" (*cheng*) means receiving and upholding; "practicing according to" (*zun*) means following in action. The metaphor of the Brahma-net illustrates that the Sages establish many gates of teaching.
The metaphor of the fish and dragons illustrates that the afflictions and karma of sentient beings are profound and heavy. "Brahma" (*fan*) means purity; "net" (*wang*) refers to a forest.

The *Shishuo* states that it can be used to capture birds and beasts. In the commentary, the character "nei" (內) may be read as "chen" (瞋, anger), serving as a contrast to the "desire and greed" mentioned below.

The *jīng* (whale) is the largest among aquatic creatures; the female is called the *ní* (shark). Cui Bao’s *Gujin Zhu* states that the large ones are a thousand *li* in length, while the small ones are several *zhang* long;
they churn the waves into snow, causing all aquatic life to tremble with fear. Their three bodies rely upon the three...

The student [should understand that] through precepts one attains the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), through concentration (*samādhi*) the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*), and through wisdom (*prajñā*) the Response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

For now, according to the text, these are generally correlated with the three trainings. However, based on the subsequent passage, the precepts are divided into three types, which correspond individually to the three bodies. The first section of the following division provides a general summary, while the second section provides a specific correlation;
finally, it concludes by returning the matter to one's own mind.
"At the beginning" (*chu zhong*) is a particle used here. The *Erya* states: "The words 'yu' and 'yuan' mean 'to say'. The "basis of the three bodies" refers to the sense of relying upon causes.
Regarding the term "vinaya" (*lüyi*), saying "to sever evil" means that there is no evil from which one does not distance oneself, thereby initiating the practice of the path to realization.

This is the cause for the virtue of cessation (*nirodha-guṇa*). It is so called because it is cultivated to accomplish the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). The *Necklace Sūtra* (*Ratnavyūha-sūtra*) states: "The precept of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*) refers to the ten *pārājikas*.
The *Commentary on the Bodhisattva Precepts* states: "The restraint of discipline (*saṃvara-śīla*) enables the mind to abide [in stability].

The sub-commentary clarifies the intent: "When virtue manifests, one immediately perceives the fundamental Dharma-body. Regarding "wholesome dharmas" (*kuśala-dharma*), the statement "to cultivate all wholesome things" means that there is no wholesome quality not included therein. That is to say...

The virtues of body, speech, and mind; the three types of wisdom consisting of hearing, reflection, and cultivation; the six perfections and myriad practices; and other such dharmas that assist the Path—these are the causes for the virtue of wisdom.

Through their cultivation, the *saṃbhogakāya* (Reward Buddha) is realized. The *Yingluo jing* states: "The gathering of wholesome dharmas refers to the eighty-four thousand dharma-gates. The *Jieshu* states:

"The gathering of wholesome dharmas brings about the attainment of the Buddha-dharmas oneself. In the commentary, it is noted that both the wholesome of restraint and the wholesome of performance encompass all [virtues].

"Excellent. Because there is nothing that is not exhausted, one gathers in sentient beings. To speak of 'compassionately aiding those with hearts' means that there are none among those born who are not saved. This gives rise to the non-abiding path; it is the cause of such benevolent virtue.

Through cultivation, the *nirmāṇakāya* (Transformation Buddha) is perfected. The *Yíngluò jīng* (Ākāśagarbha-sūtra) says: "Gathering in sentient beings refers to loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
These transformations reach all sentient beings, causing them to attain peace and happiness. The *Jièshù* (Commentary on the Precepts) says: "Gathering in sentient beings brings them to fulfillment."

In the commentary on the passage concerning "birth," it says: "The transformation buddhas are without mind because they are manifested through transformation; they respond immediately according to conditions because they are like the moon reflected in water;
their mental functions are identical because they arise from the Dharma-body and because they share the same contemplation as the Ultimate Truth."
Regarding the three returns to the One: the first two lines explain the One as being three, while the latter two lines explain the three as being one.

Although the One and the three differ, there is nothing that is not the single mind. When it is said that the "object" (境) is primordially present and not external to the mind, it means that the objects of the three bodies (*trikāya*) are none other than the practitioner’s own mind;
there is no phenomenon outside the mind, for all dharmas arise entirely from the mind.
To seek outside the mind is to distance oneself further from the Way. As the *Six Sublime Gates* states: "What is the source of all dharmas?
It is the mind of sentient beings. To be able to realize this is correct view (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*). If one seeks outside the mind, it is called false view (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*).
The *Qingliang xinyao* states: "Mind after mind acts as Buddha; there is not a single mind that is not the Buddha-mind. Everywhere the Way is perfected;
there is not a single speck of dust that is not a Buddha-land. Furthermore, a sutra says: "This mind is the Buddha; this mind creates the Buddha.

The ocean of the Buddhas' right and universal knowledge arises from the thoughts of the mind," and so forth. Regarding the convergence of a hundred deliberations, the *Zhouyi Xici* states: "Heaven..."
"What need is there for further thought or deliberation? All under heaven return to the same destination though by different paths; they reach the same unity though with a hundred deliberations.
What need is there for further thought or deliberation? The Great Master borrowed these words from him.
This extensively presents the first section of the middle [division]. The first four lines clarify that both monastics and laypeople alike must first uphold the precepts.

Regarding "the root of merit," this refers to what the sutra says: "The precepts are the root of unsurpassed bodhi. Furthermore, a sutra states: "Relying upon and because of these precepts, one attains meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and so forth.

As for "the beginning of the Way," there has never been an ordained person who did not first receive the precepts. As for "laypeople returning [to the Dharma]," this refers to [those such as] Yajñadatta...
When Śukra saw the Buddha, the Buddha first conferred the Three Refuges upon him. The elder Trapusa was the first person to receive the five precepts from the Buddha;

thus it is said that one must first reverently receive them. The following two lines describe the meaning of perfection (*yuan*): the precepts arise in accordance with the objects [of perception], and within each individual object, all three clusters (*tripiṭaka*) are fully present.
To mention one is to include all three; they are neither prior nor posterior. This is as explained below regarding how the mind manifests the precepts in their perfection.
This can be understood through integration.
Next, the section concerning the fundamental and the manifested explains the three Buddhas. First, it correctly clarifies that observing the precepts is based on the mind;

since the three [bodies] are not fixed, the three Buddhas are likewise so when fruits are induced by means of the precepts. That is to say, the Dharma-body is itself the Reward and Response bodies, and the Reward and Response bodies are themselves the Dharma-body.

Regarding the body and so forth: if one does not possess a perfect understanding, it will be difficult to investigate this matter even if cause and effect do not deviate from one another, because the three and the one are not different.
Thus, the following citation serves as proof that [the three] are not fixed [as distinct entities]. Since the birth-body is itself the Dharma-body, the sutra is none other than the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.
Its fourth fascicle states: "I have long since, for immeasurable kalpas, been free from craving and desire; this body of mine is now the Dharma-body."
The physical body conforms to the world and manifests through the eight modes of birth. The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra* also states: "One should take delight in the Buddha-body. Why is this?
The Buddha-body is precisely the Dharma-body. Furthermore, Vimalakīrti said to Ānanda: "The Tathāgata’s body is indeed the Dharma-body.
Moreover, the following passage serves as proof that [the Buddha-body] is not fixed as one: because the birth-body (*janma-kāya*) is distinct from the Dharma-body (*dharma-kāya*).
Furthermore, these differences arise from the distinct capacities of the listeners; thus, the teachings differ accordingly.

Generally speaking, within the intention behind the transformation [of beings], the first two phrases refer to how the Buddha originally taught the *Avataṃsaka* sudden doctrine for the sake of King Gṛdhrakūṭa.
This was set apart from the śrāvakas, so that only the bodhisattvas obtained the great benefit of the Dharma. As it says in the fiftieth fascicle of the *Avataṃsaka*:
For example, when the sun rises over Jambudvīpa, its light illuminates all the Mount Sumerus and other peaks.

The subsequent phrase refers to the fact that because the capacities and conditions [of the audience] were not yet sharp, the Great was set aside and the Small was bestowed; thus, the teaching was expounded gradually.

This refers to the entire period of the Dharma-teaching from the Deer Park to the Śāla Grove. What is called the "Lesser Vehicle" (Hīnayāna) is so named in contrast to the superior *Avataṃsaka*. As for the "later sessions":

This is because it was previously stated that the *Avataṃsaka* teaches the equal Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), whereas the latter [teachings] speak of gradual methods according to the capacities of beings;
hence the term "also" (*yǔ*). "Magadha" (Mójié), or alternatively "Magadha" (Mójiéti) or "Magadha" (Mójiéduō), is correctly called "Majjadhā" (Mójiétuó).

This means "the excellent, supreme, unafflicted, and ambrosial place," etc., which is precisely where the Tathāgata first attained perfect enlightenment. "Jetavana" (Qíyuán), or alternatively "Jetavana" (Qíhuán) or "Jeta" (Qí)...

*Jeta-vana-śrī-datta* (陀祇樹逝多善多) is translated collectively as "Victorious Clan" (*Śreṣṭhin*). This refers to the grove of trees donated by Prince Jeta and the park relinquished by the Elder Anāthapiṇḍada;

it was the place where the Tathāgata traveled and transformed beings. Regarding those who have fully explained the various doctrines, such as the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha of the Chen Dynasty, he established two types of teaching to encompass all doctrinal systems:
first, the Gradual (*anupūrva*), and second, the Sudden (*tadantika*). As for the term "Gradual," it refers to...

Regarding Bodhisattvas of gradual enlightenment, the Great arises from the Small; possessing the designation of "vehicle," this constitutes the Gradual Teaching, such as the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and others.
If it concerns those of direct and sudden capacity, the Great does not arise from the Small, consisting solely of the Bodhisattva Vehicle, such as the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and others.

As for the Tiantai Master Zhiyi of the Sui dynasty, he categorized these according to the five periods, five flavors, four teachings, and eight teachings, with various differences among them. As it is said:

The Chan Master Guifeng of the Tang dynasty said: "Regarding the establishment of schools and the judgment of teachings by the various masters of antiquity and the present throughout the Western Regions and this land, there are differences in their approaches to synthesis and differentiation.

Some maintain that there is but a single flavor without distinction, while others open up distinct schools and engage in critical discernment. As for those who speak of non-distinction, there are five underlying intentions."

First, because the single principle is fundamentally of one flavor, though the paths differ, they return to the same destination. Second, because the single voice universally responds, and the single rain nourishes all things alike.
Third, because the Buddha’s original intent was for the sake of a single matter. Fourth, because according to each individual passage, the various understandings differ.
Fifth, because the many types of teachings form branches and streams. Therefore, they cannot be divided. As [stated by] Bodhiruci of the Later Wei and Yao...
The Master Kumārajīva of the Qin established the teaching of the "Single Sound" (ekadhvani); this is precisely that meaning. Regarding the analysis and discernment of its fundamental principles:

First, although the principle is of a single flavor, the explanations have varying depths. Second, although the Buddha employs a single sound, the teachings differ according to the capacities of sentient beings.

Third, the original intent has not yet been fully expressed, as the words follow the intentions of others. Fourth, while the words possess both general and specific meanings, they are explained here through their manifest significance. Fifth, it is due to [the following] discernment...
1. Regarding provisional and ultimate [teachings]: because they do not abide in secondary branches or streams. 2. Regarding the secret words of the six kings:

because the words are the same while the matters are different. 3. Regarding those who do not understand the Buddha’s intent: taking the profound as shallow when it concerns great benefit, and taking the shallow as profound when it concerns empty merit.
4. Regarding all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas: because they also distinguish for themselves. For these reasons, they are thus divided. If one relies on the Great Master Xianshou...

The Master [Wonhyo] synthesizes these into five categories: first, the Hīnayāna teaching; second, the Initial Mahāyāna teaching; third, the Final Mahāyāna teaching; fourth, the Sudden One-Vehicle teaching; and fifth, the Perfect teaching.

Although the aforementioned schools differ in their doctrinal classifications, they all rely upon the sūtras and śāstras to distinguish them, with the underlying intent being to return to the principle of the single essence. "Mirror" (kyǒng) signifies clarity and illumination.
In the section on "Discerning Nature and Characteristics," the first part consists of an upper clause that concludes the preceding and a lower clause that introduces what follows.

In the subsequent part, which "Manifests the Benefits," the first six lines point to what was taught within the conditions—namely, the causes and effects of cultivation and nature, the three types of precepts and the three Buddhas, and so forth—and the perfect understanding and perfect cultivation.
This is intended to cause the practitioner’s mental flower to blossom through these verbal teachings, just like the light of a lamp; thereafter...
This explains the nature and characteristics of the Three Jewels as being of one essence, so that the practitioner’s mind remains free from attachment;

thus, the conclusion below states briefly that "the raft may be abandoned. "Raft" (*bān*) refers to a raft; furthermore, a structure woven of wood is called a *pái*, while a structure woven of bamboo is called a *bǎi*.

These are the means for crossing rivers and streams. As the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* says: "Know my teaching of the Dharma to be like the parable of the raft. Even the Dharma should be relinquished.

"To abandon [even] the Dharma, how much more so that which is not the Dharma. This is correct. Furthermore, it may be said that the first four lines describe the purpose of their coming, while the latter four lines reveal the essential purport.

In the first section of the "Manifesting the Nature and Characteristics," it states that one who knows the nature is inherently pure is called a Buddha; this is because they are able to awaken to it themselves.

Furthermore, as for the mind as a phenomenon, it is wondrous beyond thought. It stands solitary and independent. When the Buddhas attain this mind, it is called *bodhi*, yet it has never been said to be pure.
When sentient beings are deluded regarding this mind, it is called birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), yet it has likewise never possessed any defilement.
Yet, within that state of non-perception, there is a sudden arising of perception which is forcibly designated as "Buddha. Since the Buddha is thus, so too are the Dharma and the Sangha.
The Three Jewels are of one essence, yet they are also forcibly divided into three. It would suffice simply to know that non-defilement is the Dharma and non-obstruction is the Sangha.
Now, the following provides a general indication of the Three Jewels; alternatively, it may separately manifest Perfect Enlightenment. Nevertheless, the nature of enlightenment is eternally abiding.
Sentient beings are mired in delusion; therefore, it is called "non-awakening" (*abodha*). Because they attain understanding through the teaching, it is called "initial awakening" (*ādi-bodhi*).
When that which is understood is not yet perfected, it is called "equal awakening" (*samyak-sambodhi*). When it is ultimately true and eternal, it is called "wondrous awakening" (*vicitra-bodhi*).

While these are spoken of as having a sequence, in principle there is no sequence. However, the essence of nature is perfectly interfused and nothing is left unaccomplished. Cultivation and nature are non-dual; sentient beings and Buddhas are of one suchness. All phenomena are entirely...
The mind manifests: it may be called contemplating the one mind and seeing all minds and all dharmas;
contemplating one dharma and seeing all dharmas and all minds; contemplating bodhi and nirvana and seeing all afflictions and birth-and-death;
contemplating afflictions and birth-and-death and seeing bodhi and nirvana; contemplating one Buddha and seeing all sentient beings and all Buddhas.
Contemplating a single sentient being, one perceives all Buddhas and all sentient beings as neither internal nor external, neither different nor identical;
this is called the wondrous essence of the single nature, which is inconceivable.
If those who study, contemplate, explain, and practice can truly penetrate this, then how could the Three Jewels of the One Body be far off? Yet most people do not believe in this single Dharma.
To sink one's own spirit is as described in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*: Sun Jing was a man from Langye who habitually read the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Upon seeing that it stated one becomes a Buddha from the very moment of generating the bodhicitta, he gave rise to slander and disparagement.

Just as he was about to stretch out his hands and feet, the ground beneath him suddenly began to crack slowly; Jing’s body fell instantly, and he was reborn trapped in hell. To this day there is a pit there known as "Sun Jing."
This is the *naraka* (hell). A true practitioner of the Way should believe in their own spiritual nature and need not seek it externally.

Within the section on exhortation: the first four lines instruct one to practice diligently; the subsequent lines cite worldly examples to encourage the pursuit of the Way. Regarding the initial two lines, they direct one to cultivate according to the teachings;
the final two lines ensure that one does not succumb to negligence or indolence. As for the phrase "The world says," this refers to the *Shangshu* (Book of Documents).
This truly refers to the sovereign of the time. The commentary on that passage states: "If a sage does not contemplate what is good, he becomes a madman;
if a madman can contemplate what is good, he becomes a sage. This means that Jie and Zhou were not actually insane or foolish; they perished simply because they did not contemplate what was good.
As the ancients said: "Yao and Shun flourished through their outspokenness; Jie and Zhou met with ruin through their sycophancy. This is precisely it.

In the midst of these questions and answers that follow upon the difficulty: this question arises because the preceding mind is fundamentally pure; one who awakens to and understands this absence of error is called a Buddha, and thus [the opponent] makes this provisional assumption.
The first two phrases censure him for lacking a basis; the next two phrases state that ordinary people of the lower realms are unable to give rise to such wisdom;

the final two phrases point out his arrogance and delusion. As for the initial address "You" (*qīng*), it is like the way people today address the worthy; in antiquity, there were no fixed conventions for its usage, following general precedent.
All address him as such; it was like the case of Meng Xi’s father in the Han dynasty, whom people of the time called "Meng Qing.
When Miti admonished the assembly, he also said, "O you gentlemen (qing). Subsequent emperors and kings monopolized this title for their subordinates, so that none dared to usurp its use.

As for "the mind that cognizes thought after thought," "cognition" (shi) refers to deluded cognition which, when awakened, becomes the true nature (xing). It is called "cognition" because of delusion, for it encompasses both good and evil.
"Non-intelligence" refers not to the supramundane noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*). It is cited from the *Zhuangzi*: "In the Northern Ocean there is a fish; its name is Kun.
The size of the Kun is such that one cannot know how many thousands of li it measures. It transforms into a bird; its name is Peng.
The back of the Peng is such that one cannot know how many thousands of li it measures. It soars upward in a rage... [The passage continues: "Its..."
Its wings were like clouds hanging from the sky. This bird, when it makes its journey by sea, intends to migrate to the Southern Abyss. The Southern Abyss is the Great Pond of Heaven.
When the Penglai migrates to the Southern Abyss, it strikes the water for three thousand li and soars upon the whirlwind (fúyáo) for ninety thousand li.
This is intended to mean that ordinary beings cannot become Buddhas immediately.
In the direct response, there are two parts: first, the direct answer to the question; second, the exhortation to develop understanding and practice as follows.

Regarding the first part, the initial two lines contrast the path of the mind with the mountain, establishing the relationship between the dharma and its metaphor. Therefore, from "ten thousand" (*wan*) downward, worldly matters are compared with the number of kalpas.
Within the first section, because the Buddha-dharma is so sublime, it is truly difficult to exhaustively fathom; the subsequent line states:
The mind is truly easy to seek; it is only because one lacks the clarity of self-insight that one remains so deluded. As the former masters have said:

"Nothing is more immediate or easier than one's own mind, yet when it comes to departing from death and entering birth, one remains entirely unaware. Regarding the second couplet, "to serve as the foundation for the mountain":
this refers to the basket of earth used in construction. As the *Analects* says: "It is like building a mountain; if one basket of earth has not yet been added, the work is not yet complete."
"Ceasing is my ceasing. This is like leveling the ground: even if one has only covered it with a single basketful of earth, moving forward is my advancing.

A person of sincerity must not abandon their path midway; this is an analogy. To speak of "the Buddha's initial thought" refers to the beginning. To speak of "the merit of three kalpas" refers to the end.
Only by not allowing thoughts to cease moment by moment can one reach that goal. Thus, the Avataṃsaka Sūtra says: "The initial..."

"At the moment of generating the aspiration for enlightenment, one immediately attains perfect awakening. Furthermore, it says: "In a single thought-moment, one universally contemplates immeasurable eons;

there is no going, no coming, and no abiding. Thus understanding the events of the three periods of time, one transcends all expedient means and accomplishes the ten directions. This is the teaching of the Dharma.
In the section on comparative measurement, regarding the phrase "the first step," Laozi said: "A journey of a thousand li begins with a single step;

the root that encircles a man's arms begins with a tiny sprout. Now, when we speak of ten thousand li, it is merely a figurative way of referring to the three *kalpas*, which are the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.
This translates as "incalculable periods of time. As for the mention of "three," this is based on the period during which Śākyamuni cultivated the path of a bodhisattva.
From Śākyamuni in the past back to Vipaśyin, he encountered seventy-five thousand Buddhas; this is called the first asaṃkhyeya kalpa.
From Vipaśyin back to Dīpaṃkara, he encountered seventy-six thousand Buddhas; this is called the second asaṃkhyeya kalpa.
From Dīpaṃkara back to Śikhin, he encountered seventy-seven thousand Buddhas; this is called the third asaṃkhyeya kalpa. Therefore, they are collectively referred to as "three."
It is an eon (*kalpa*).

Next, regarding the opening of the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*): this is spoken in reference to the "opening, showing, awakening, and entering" (*kai-shi-o-nyū*) of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

Those who constantly walk according to this mind are the Three Jewels of the One Body (*ekakāya-triratna*). "Opening and showing" refers to the Tathāgata’s revelation; "awakening and entering" refers to the previous sentient beings obtaining benefit.

It is simply that sincerity arises from within rather than coming from without; these are merely different ways of expressing the same thing. If one can thoroughly realize that the three realms are mind-only and all phenomena are consciousness-only, then one will know that there are no phenomena outside the mind.
All hundredfold deliberations ultimately converge upon the subject who worships and the object of worship, which arise solely from the mind itself.

Therefore, Nanyue said: "Seek only within yourself; do not look for it elsewhere. Even if you seek it, you shall not find it; even if you were to find it," [it would be nothing other than your own mind].
This is not true. One should know that this mind is fully realized only by the sages. If an ordinary person were to awaken to it, they would be a sage.
Nevertheless, as it is said in the *Prajñāpāramitā*: "Only a Buddha can fathom the depths of the great ocean of wisdom."
In the citation from scripture, the *Sūtra of Contemplation of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life* states: "The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, are the body of the Dharma-realm;
they enter into the thoughts and minds of all sentient beings. Therefore, when you contemplate the Buddha with your thoughts and minds... Master Zhiyi remarked:
"Regarding 'entering into the thoughts and minds of all sentient beings,' it means that when the minds of sentient beings are pure, the Dharmakāya manifests with sovereign freedom."
Therefore, it is said that he enters into the thoughts and minds of sentient beings, like the sun shining in the sky, its reflection appearing in a hundred rivers. It is further stated:
"Having attained this Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha, because one understands how to enter through thought and response, it is said that he enters into the thoughts and minds.

As for the phrase "this mind creates the Buddha," the Buddha is fundamentally non-existent; he exists because the mind is pure. Furthermore, by means of this samādhi, the mind ultimately achieves Buddhahood.
As for the statement "this mind is Buddha": previously, one heard that the Buddha is fundamentally non-existent and exists only because the mind is pure.
Thinking, therefore, that these two are distinct and separate, one says that there is no Buddha outside of this mind. This serves as proof that the original nature of the mind is inherently pure;
when one realizes and understands this without error, it is called "Buddha."
In the concluding exhortation, the first four lines clarify the nature of the mind; by practicing this moment after moment without ceasing, one will surely reach accomplishment.

"Gathering the thoughts" means to follow and honor the instructions. "Pure and clear" means that awakening has found its ultimate destination. The final four lines implicitly contrast the mundane and non-Buddhist paths:
they do not follow the True Path, but forget themselves to seek elsewhere, turning their backs on the Way to pursue worldly blessings. The word *fǔ* (甫) is used here as a particle of transition.
How could those who seek [the truth] through external means ever be considered as practicing the Way? They may perhaps be said to understand through words;

those who speak of worldly merit include, for example, ordinary people observing the five or eight precepts, practicing charity and benevolence, or non-Buddhists practicing seated meditation and cultivating concentration.

Although their power and ability do not reach the realization of non-self, these ultimately constitute worldly merit, as in the case of Udraka Rāmaputra and others. Therefore, the following four lines [state this].
To distinguish between gain and loss: Śāriputra was so named because his mother, Śārī, possessed an excellent body;

thus he was called "Son of Śārī" (Śāriputra), or alternatively "Son of Śāri" (Śārisuta), because his mother’s eyes were like those of a śāri crane. Regarding the term "unthinkable," as stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 14:
"Śāriputra cultivated the bodhisattva path for sixty kalpas when he wished to cross the River of Giving. At that time—
There was a beggar who begged for his eyes. Śāriputra said, "These are of no use; why do you seek them?
If you require my body or my wealth, I shall give them to you. The man replied, "I do not need your body, nor your wealth;
I only wish to obtain your eyes. If you truly practice the giving of *dāna*, give me your eyes. At that time, Śāriputra...
He plucked out one eye and gave it to him. When the beggar received the eye, he looked at Śāriputra with anger and loathing;
he spat upon it, threw it to the ground, and then stepped on it with his foot. Śāriputra reflected, saying: "People such as this are difficult to deliver.
This eye is truly of no use, yet he forcibly demands it; having obtained it, he now tramples it underfoot—how can anyone be so wicked?"
"These people cannot be saved; it would be better for me to save myself and escape birth and death early. Having reflected thus, he withdrew from the bodhisattva path and turned toward the Hīnayāna.
This is what is meant by "not reaching the other shore," and so forth. Nanda is the name of a woman; this translates as "Joy.
Regarding the phrase "to rectify one's thoughts and extract the spirit," the tenth fascicle of the *Xiányú jīng* (Sūtra on the Wise and the Foolish) states: "When the Buddha was in Śrāvastī..."
There was a woman named Nanda who sustained herself by begging. Seeing the kings, officials, and common people making offerings to the Buddha and the Sangha, she thought to herself:
"Due to my past transgressions, I have been born into poverty and low status. Although I have encountered this field of merit, I have no seed [of wealth] to offer.
She then went out to beg and managed to obtain a single coin as a small offering. Carrying it to an oil merchant's house, she explained her intentions in detail. The oil merchant...
Feeling compassion, [the man] doubled the amount of oil he gave. Having received it, the man was overjoyed; with this, he was able to prepare a single lamp and offered it to the World-Honored One.
He then made this vow: "I am currently poor, yet I have used this small lamp to make an offering to the Buddha.
