By this merit, may I, in future lives, obtain the lamp of wisdom to extinguish the defiled darkness of all sentient beings. Having made this vow, he prostrated before the Buddha.

He departed. Thus it continued until the end of the night; all the other lamps were extinguished, yet this one alone remained burning. At that time, it was Maudgalyāyana’s turn to serve as the day-duty attendant.
Desiring to extinguish it, he raised his hand and fanned it, and again he fanned it with his robe, but the light of the lamp was not diminished.
The Buddha said to Maudgalyāyana, "This lamp cannot be moved by you, a śrāvaka. Even if the waters of the four great oceans [were used]..."
He poured it over [the fire], yet even the Vairambha winds could not extinguish it. This was a gift bestowed by one who has resolved upon the Great Mind (mahācitta).

After the Buddha had spoken thus, the maiden Nandā returned, prostrated herself with her head at his feet, and the Buddha immediately conferred upon her the prediction that, after two asaṃkhyeya kalpas in a future age, she would become a Buddha named Dīpamkara, fully endowed with the ten titles. This is [the account].
This recognizes the fault of Śāriputra’s deviation from the Great [Vehicle] and the merit of Nanda’s conformity to principle.

Regarding these two types of reliance on principle, a question is asked: "Principle has its great and small aspects, and the teaching has its partial and perfect aspects. Now, this reliance on principle—is it of the Great [Vehicle] or the Small [Vehicle]?

Furthermore, three hundred and sixty-five thousand monastics, both monks and nuns, were returned to lay life. After the Dharma had been suppressed for two years, Emperor Wu passed away and Emperor Xuanzong ascended the throne.

The reign title was changed to Dazhong, and [the Dharma] was restored. This occurred after the time of the Patriarchs; however, it is not mentioned in the *Wen* (Commentary). It is said that after ten thousand years, there would be no further transmission.
If one calculates this according to the three periods of the True, Semblance, and Final [Dharma], then for twelve thousand years there will be no transmission.

As the *Qinglong jieshi* (Exegesis of the Blue Dragon) states: "There are, in total, three stages during which the Dharma abides in the world, wherein both the Teaching (*śāsana*) and the Practice (*pratipatti*) are fully present."

The period of the realization of the fruit is called the True Dharma (*saddharma*). When there are teachings and practices, but no realization of the fruit, it is called the Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpakadharma*).
When only the teachings remain, while practice and the realization of the fruit are absent, it is called the Final Dharma (*antadharmakāla*). As for the ultimate extinction:

when the human lifespan increases to sixty thousand years, the various Arhats will transform into fire and burn away the sutra scrolls of the great trichiliocosm; at that time, there will be no further transmission. Now...

The phrase "ten thousand years" is merely a general approximation. The expression "the end of the mandate of the cosmic cycle" (*lishu luku zhong*) is borrowed from the "Yao Yi" chapter of the *Lunyu*.
When the era of Maitreya opens, it refers to Maitreya’s descent to birth. The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "The lifespan of a son is twice that of his father;

when it increases to eighty thousand years, the kalpa of destruction ends and Maitreya arises. The older tradition says: "Upon reaching the tenth sub-eon of decrease, human lifespan reaches six [thousand years]."
When the human lifespan is ten thousand years, Maitreya will appear in the world; some say he appears when it is seventy thousand years. *Huizhenjie* (The Compendium of True Understanding) states:

"The Dharma of Śākyamuni’s transformation lasted sixty thousand years; when Pratyekabuddhas appeared in the world, it was at seventy thousand years. Only thereafter did Maitreya descend," and so forth.

This refers to the maturation of conditions, meaning that there is a response when the capacity [of sentient beings] is ripe. *Daohui* (The Assembly of the Way) states that the sages do not differ [in their timing]. Furthermore, once the karmic conditions are met...
It is ripe; one should appropriately realize the Holy Path.
In the concluding summary, the first four lines conclude the preceding text. Therefore, the following citation of the text exhorts the cultivation of the Jewel of the Path.

Regarding "the Path resides in the mind," the mind is taken as the subject that realizes, and the Path as the object realized. This depends solely upon being firm, resolute, and courageous; why concern oneself with whether one is old or young?
This is comparable to middle age. As for the statement that "faith must be maintained," how could this apply solely to Buddhism?
Confucians also say, "Without faith, a person cannot stand. A mirror is clarity itself.
In the explanation of names through the perspective of manifested characteristics (*nirmāṇa-lakṣaṇa*): Śākyamuni as the Buddha refers to the six-foot body within the royal palace;

the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) as the Dharma refers to the propagation of the teachings on the truths in order to manifest the principle of cessation; and the prior wisdom, when fully exhausted, constitutes the Saṃgha—this defines the Saṃgha by way of the Dharma.

Some speak of the five *cakras* and so forth; this refers directly to human beings. As for what is called the "transformed appearance" (*nirmāṇa-lakṣaṇa*), it refers to the Tathāgata’s descent from Tuṣita Heaven riding upon the auspicious white elephant to take birth—this is the appearance of his teaching and transformation.
The specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) have been distinguished as previously explained. Regarding the determination of the essential substance (*svabhāva*) in the first section:
the substance is impermanent because it belongs to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). The four marks (*lakṣaṇa*) are precisely birth, aging, sickness, and death. The old [translation] says:

[The four phases of existence are] arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing. The phrase "more than a thousand years" is stated as a general approximation; however, according to the date this text was composed, more than sixteen hundred years have already passed.
The practice of commemorating the distant past originates from the *Analects*. Nevertheless, within the Buddha-dharma, there are four occasions for commemorating the distant past:

namely, the descent into birth, the attainment of enlightenment, the turning of the Wheel of Dharma, and the entry into parinirvāṇa. Because it expresses a heart that turns toward [the Buddha], it is called "uplifted reverence."
The following sections all clarify the practice of honoring the distant past with reverent devotion. Thus, while in the world, he preached the Dharma to deliver sentient beings;
after his passing, he manifested various forms to manifest his transformation. In every case, he extended himself to benefit others; his benevolence and virtue are beyond measure.
Regarding the phrase "in the benefit for the world" and so forth, within this *bhadrakalpa* (Auspicious Aeon), there are twenty periods of increase and decrease (*utsarpiṇī* and *avasarpiṇī*).
During the ninth period of decrease, when the human lifespan was eighty-four thousand years, it decreased by one year every hundred years.

When the lifespan had decreased to sixty thousand years, Krakucchanda Buddha appeared in the world; he is the first Buddha of this *bhadrakalpa*. At the time when the lifespan was forty thousand years...
When the lifespan was twenty thousand years, Kanakamuni Buddha appeared in the world; when it had reached one hundred years, Śākyamuni Buddha arose.
The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "This period of abiding is called the Bhadrakalpa (Auspicious Aeon).

Among the twenty cycles, during the ninth aeon of decrease, when the lifespan was sixty-four thousand, twenty thousand, and ten thousand years respectively, the three Buddhas—Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni, and Kāśyapa—appeared. [The fourth, Śākyamuni, appears] at the time of the hundred-year lifespan."

Śākyamuni appeared in the world. It was asked: "Why is it that the lifespan of the Tathāgata Śākya is so extremely short, and why does he arise in the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*), unlike other Buddhas?
The answer was: "As for his short lifespan, it is because the human life span is one hundred years, and thus the conditions of the faculties (*indriya*) have now matured.
As for his dwelling in the five turbidities, it is to repay past karma. The *Mahāvaipulya-dhāraṇī-sūtra* states: "In the past, there was once a certain..."
The bhikṣu named Śuddhajīva abided in right view and offered flowers as an act of worship. There was another bhikṣu named Dharmacārin who abided in wrong view;

though he sat in the attainment of the four dhyānas and constantly preached the doctrine of emptiness, asserting that Prajñāpāramitā is supreme, he slandered Śuddhajīva’s Dharma, claiming it was not the teaching of Śuddhajīva.
He refused to offer the flowers he had received. Because I uttered these words, for sixty thousand years I shall always...
He was without the faculty of taste, and so on, until he attained Buddhahood while dwelling amidst the five turbidities. Who was this person? It was none other than Śākyamuni.

For this reason, the following clarifies the phase of transformation (*nirmāṇa-kāya*): the Teacher capable of preaching is the fourth Śākyamuni appearing in the world, who preaches the Dharma to transform sentient beings and enables them to cross the ocean of suffering.
Because he responds precisely to the appointed time, he is said to have "met the period. As the *Karmavācanā-vidhi* states: "The Great Teaching..."

This refers to the fulfillment of the appointed time. The opening two lines clarify the treasury of teachings that are expounded. The first line identifies the essence of the partial and gradual teachings.

Regarding the term "Eightfold Path" (*aṣṭāṅgamārga*): its essence is so called because it is free from the erroneous. Furthermore, it is called the "Eightfold Noble Path" (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*) because one attains the state of a noble one (*ārya*) by means of these eight factors.
These are not outside the Three Trainings (*triśikṣā*), though they are divided into eight: namely, right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, and right effort.

Right mindfulness, right concentration, and so forth. The first two belong to wisdom (*prajñā*); the middle three belong to ethical discipline (*śīla*); the latter three belong to meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

"Opening" means to reveal and instruct, enabling others to awaken and enter [the path]; this is the skillful means (*upāya*) for entering through successive stages of cultivation. The subsequent phrase sets forth the essence of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching (*yuan-dun jiao*).
This is the original intent of the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world; hence the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "Directly abandoning the skillful means, but..."
It speaks of the Unsurpassed Way. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "The Tathāgatas of the ten directions follow one and the same path. It also says:
"The Bhagavans of the ten directions share a single road to the gate of Nirvāṇa. The *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* says: "A straightforward mind is the Way. All these express this same meaning.
This refers to the application of the proximate, lower, manifest teachings (Hīnayāna). Humans, devas, and noble sages are the capacities to be saved; they are mired in the mud of the five desires.

One will then fall into the four evil destinies. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The turbid desires of the world can bind the human mind like falling into deep mud, making it difficult to rescue.

The ferry and raft of the sages and saints—on a large scale, these are the three stages of worthiness and the ten stages of sainthood; on a small scale, they are the seven stages of worthiness and the four stages of sainthood—are the raft and oar.
This establishes the intent behind the teaching. Regarding the Three Jewels as explained through principle (*li*), this refers to the Buddha of manifested characteristics (*huaxiangfo*).
That which is taught is intended to lead one toward the direct and equal Way. That the True Principle abides eternally is the fundamental realization (*pratyātma-adhigama*).
To "mount the provisional (*upāya*) to govern the real" refers to the descent into birth. If we interpret the meaning of the text:

one mounts the reality of the principle-body (*dharmatā-kāya*) and governs the provisional aspect of transformative phenomena (*nirmāṇa-lakṣaṇa*), appearing in the world to preach the aforementioned dharmas. Here, "mounting" (*sheng*) means "governing" (*yu*). According to other texts:
The nine realms belong to the provisional, while the Buddha-realm is the real. Thus, a sutra says: "The three stages of worthiness and the ten stages of sagehood dwell in retributive fruition;
only the Buddha alone dwells in the eternal abode. Furthermore, one should know that within the provisional there is the real, and within the real there is the provisional.
Since the provisional and the real are non-dual, the fundamental principle and its manifested forms are originally without distinction. The latter two lines clarify the perception of sentient beings.

[The Master] said: "I believe that these holy men have no different refuge; therefore, they are called 'loosely liberated' (*suxie*). Furthermore, they can be constrained by the precepts, purify their minds through concentration and wisdom, and practice according to the teachings;
thus they are called 'loosely liberated. 'Loose' (*su*) refers to the loosening of [deluded] principles, and 'liberated' (*jie*) refers to thorough understanding.

Since the three trainings are clear and they rely upon the Buddha’s words, they are called 'sons' (*zi*). The six phrases following 'receiving the Way' refer to the honor accorded to the person and the Dharma."

"Victorious. This refers to the ability to cultivate and thereby attain benefit; it is the essence of the Path, which is limpid, fundamental purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*). "Limpid" means pure and clear; "non-existent" (*wu*) means empty and quiescent (*śūnyatā*);

"fundamental purity" is the state of ultimate attainment. Regarding the metaphor of the trap and net: it means that by knowing the nature of all phenomena (*dharma*) to be empty, one’s insight becomes void and penetrating, no longer lingering in the traces of the teachings.
"Matters and meanings" refer to phenomenal characteristics (*nimitta*); "divine function" refers to mental wisdom (*citta-jñāna*); and "radiance" refers to—

It is not obscure. The first line clarifies understanding; the subsequent two lines clarify that by relying on this to practice, one attains awakening and entry, thereby being able to exhaust birth and death—this is the arising of practice.
This concludes the three sections on the middle [benefit]. The first two lines clarify the time of the eighty-fold proclamation of extinction (*parinirvāṇa*).

This refers to the passage in the Sūtra: "Today, at midnight, I shall enter parinirvāṇa," and so forth. This signifies that the conditions for the Sahā world have been exhausted and the work of transformation is finished;
it is appropriate to manifest extinction. *Lóng* (隆) means "to complete. Next, the following four lines concern the benefit after his passing. The first two lines intend to clarify the Dharma...
The body is originally without form or characteristics, yet it was able to manifest its appearance once again at the assembly of Nirvāṇa;
one must know that this is because the Dharmakāya does not forget. The following section explicitly clarifies the benefits [of the Buddha] after his passing.

As for the statement that "the traces of transformation do not vanish," it means that [the influence] flows down to the twelve thousand years of the future, such that the remaining wind [of his teaching] is never replaced—*mín* meaning to cease or be extinguished. The third section below distinguishes [these points].
He manifested his traces of transformation; by fragmenting his body, he gave rise to faith, as exemplified by the eight *droṇas* and four *āḍhakas* of *śarīra*.

He preserved his divine power in its entirety, as seen in the *Śrīlā* relic, which refers to the eyes, teeth, hair, nails, and so forth. Among these, the eyes are the most essential; therefore, they are held aloft.

Yet, from the Buddha’s descent into birth to his manifestation of parinirvāṇa, the influence of his merit in benefiting and saving others is inconceivable and beyond discussion; words cannot express it.
This person’s kindness and virtue are so profound that they do not fall within the scope of the four debts of gratitude; since it is difficult to repay them, how else can one express thanks?

In the section on exhortation, the phrase "therefore, when one encounters" means that the subsequent state arises from the preceding one. To first prepare this mind is precisely the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*). If...

If one practices this without ceasing, one will attain the power of faith (*śraddhā-bala*). If one is endowed with the powers of the faculties (*indriya-bala*), what task could not be accomplished? "By" (*you*) refers to the cause or reason;
"commission" (*wei*) means to entrust, to approach, or to understand thoroughly; it also implies being well-versed in or familiar with.
In the "Preface to the Intent" (*Renchi xuyi*), the first four lines clarify the person and the Dharma through mutual manifestation. The first two lines trace back to the person;
the subsequent two lines investigate the Dharma. Although the words used throughout are not distinct, the positions held by the preceding and following sections differ.

"Ten thousand years" refers to time; "the three dharmas" refers to the gates of the Dharma. The phrase "opening the positions" refers to opening the positions of the three dharmas, which are precisely the Three Jewels.

Alternatively, those who argue based on the three periods of the True Dharma, the Semblance Dharma, and the Final Dharma are merely conflating the terminology used for successive generations in later times.

Consequently, they project the merit downward and attribute it to the monastic community. By correlating each generation with its respective era and each location with its specific territory, they demonstrate that were it not for the Sangha, the Buddha-dharma would have vanished;
this clarifies that among the Three Jewels of the institutional tradition, the Jewel of the Sangha is primary.
In the first section of the "Manifestation of Signs" (Shixiang), the first two lines clarify the existence of the Buddha, while the latter two lines state the absence of the Sangha.
Emperor Wu of Han was the sixth sovereign of the Former Han; his majesty shook the four seas and the myriad states came to court, hence he is described as "venerably prosperous.
As for those who heard the name of the Buddha, it was at the beginning of the Yuanshou era, when he commanded Huo Qubing to launch a northern campaign against the Xiongnu, passing through Juyan.
The King of Huitu (pronounced "chu") presented a golden man (who was none other than the Buddha), whom he regarded as a great deity and enshrined in the Gandhakuṭī Palace (Gānquán Gōng).

He offered incense and performed rites of worship before it. Three years later, while dredging the Kūṇing Lake (Kūnmíng Chí), black ashes were discovered. When Emperor Wu questioned Dongfang Shuo about this, Shuo replied, "This is not something I can know.
Your Majesty should ask the foreign barbarian practitioners from the Western Regions (those who have heard the name of the Buddha). At that time, if...
There is a tradition among the monastics that the Three Jewels had already been circulating in the world; however, because there was no Sangha, no one was able to open up its initial path.
Therefore, it is said that [the Dharma] was exhausted.

Within the section on the "Broad Manifestation" (*Hongxiang*), the first two phrases clarify the convergence of the times and conditions through which kings and ministers from afar came to admire [the Dharma], leading to the following description of how the Triple Gem was first established in this land. Regarding the initial statement, "Xianzong opened the Dharma":

this refers to the second sovereign of the Later Han, Emperor Ming, whose posthumous title was Xianzong. He was the fourth son of Emperor Guangwu. In the third year of Yongping, the Gengshen year, he...

In that year, he dreamed of golden men and other such visions. Fan Zhenyi submitted a memorial, saying: "Your servant has examined the *Weizhi yiji* (Record of Extraordinary Events) of the Book of Zhou and learned that a Sage is born in the Western Regions, and that one thousand years later, his teachings will flow into this land. Is it not certain that what Your Majesty dreamed must be of him?
In the seventh year, the Jiazi year, he dispatched Cai Yin and Qin Jing to go forth and welcome the Buddha-dharma. Cai Yin was sent on this mission to seek it out; upon arriving...
In the kingdom of the Great Yuezhi (pronounced "Zhi"), he met Kāśyapa Mātanga and Zhu Falan.
In the tenth year, the *dingmao* year, the Han envoy returned, bringing about the great flourishing of the Buddha-dharma; thus it is said that the Dharma was opened. "Huaxu" refers to India;
according to Ying Shao and others, it is indeed India. When the Three Jewels first began to circulate within China, Kāśyapa and Zhu arrived.

As for "rituals," this refers to Kāśyapa Mātanga and others who followed the Han envoys into Luoyang and presented to Emperor Ming a painted image of Śākyamuni on white silk, which was carried by a white horse, along with the *Sūtra in Forty-two Sections*.
As for "opening up worldly affairs," this refers to Kāśyapa Mātanga manifesting his supernatural powers.
Having prevailed over Chu Shanxin and others in the contest of dharma, he subsequently opened the minds of the laity and accomplished the work of the Buddha-dharma.
Those who were inspired with faith and returned their hearts to the Way—such as the Daoist masters of the Five Peaks whom Falan preached the Dharma to—were made to cast off their crowns and hairpins.
He sought to leave the household life. This truly relies on the Three Jewels to abide; among them, the Jewel of the Sangha is placed first. What follows clarifies the Jewel of the Dharma:
"name" refers to names, and "phrase" refers to the meaning of phrases; these belong to that which expresses. "Principle" refers to true emptiness, which is that which is expressed.
"Name," "phrase," and "words" are called "teachings"; this is merely a variation of the terminology. This is because principle is fundamentally beyond words and is not [expressed by] words.
If its principle were not made manifest, and if there were no representation, from what source could awakening and understanding arise? This is precisely what the Sūtra means when it says:

"If the Buddha-dharma is not spoken by someone, even one possessed of wisdom cannot understand it. Below this, the text distinguishes the reflected image of the Jewel of the Buddha, namely clay niches and molded statues.
This refers to the Buddha as the Sustainer (the *saṃbhogakāya*).

In the section on "Concluding the Indication," the preceding part clarifies not encountering the Buddha of Transformation (*nirmāṇakāya*), while the subsequent part clarifies the good fortune of beholding the Buddha as the Sustainer.

Regarding the first section on the "Precious Body" (*ratnakāya*): first, it demonstrates that the Sustainer is without effort. The first two lines clarify that the Buddha-dharma belongs to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). [The text continues with] "Possessing... below.

The first phrase clarifies that the Sangha-jewel belongs to the realm of outflows and defilement; the subsequent phrase universally concludes that it is without [inherent] function. However, what follows reveals that, from the perspective of the fundamental source, the former is superior.
Taking the Jewel of Principle as the root and the institutional maintenance as the branch, to subsume the branch back into the root is the meaning that emerges.

Regarding the first four lines of the verse, they explain the general worldly custom. Below, a scriptural passage is cited as proof. First, concerning the term *zhēng* (徵): it means to seek out or to verify.

Although a messenger is not as honorable as the king himself, because he acts as the king’s envoy, one must not fail to show respect by verifying his status based on the lowliness of his physical appearance.
Alternatively, the character *zhēng* (徵) may be an error for *kǒng* (恐). The scripture referred to is the *Candragarbha-sūtra*, specifically from its ninth section.

The Chapter on Spreading [the Dharma] throughout Jambudvīpa. It says therein: "Within my Dharma, there may be those who, though they have shaved their hair and beards and wear the saṃghāṭī robe, violate the prohibitions and precepts and act contrary to the Dharma; they are merely called 'bhikṣus' by name.
If there is a donor who gives alms and offerings to such a bhikṣu who has broken the precepts, and protects and sustains him, I say that this person still attains [merit]."
It is an immeasurable mass of great merit. Why is this? Because it is still able to benefit many sentient beings;
how much more so now that I am currently present in the world! For example, just as pure gold is a priceless treasure, if there were no pure gold, silver would be priceless;
if there were no silver, brass would be priceless; and if there were no brass, counterfeit jewels would be priceless.
Price. If there were no counterfeit jewels, then red and white copper, iron, tin, lead, and pewter would be considered priceless treasures.
In this way, among all worlds, the Jewel of the Buddha is supreme; if there were no Jewel of the Buddha, the Pratyekabuddha would be supreme; and so on, until:

if there were no Pratyekabuddhas, then Arhats, other noble ones, those who have attained meditative concentration, those who uphold the precepts, those who violate the precepts, and those who have shaved their hair [would be supreme].
Wearing the *kāṣāya*, one who bears the name of a *bhikṣu* is an unsurpassed treasure. Compared to the ninety-five kinds of heterodox paths, he is the most honored and foremost;
he should receive the offerings of the world as a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*). Why is this? Because he is able to show sentient beings what is pleasing and what is to be feared.
If there are those who protect, support, nourish, and establish him, that person will before long attain abiding on the stage of patience (*kṣānti-bhūmi*). Therefore, [it is said] below:
The correspondence with the Dharma can be understood accordingly.
Regarding the section on "Respectful Reverence": the first four lines clarify the harm of irreverence. "Place" (*so*) refers to the location; "entrusted" (*ji*) means to entrust or rely upon.

Therefore, the subsequent lines clarify the benefits of maintaining reverence through both physical form and mind. Physical form pertains to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and belongs to the realm of phenomena (*dharma*); the mind pertains to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) and belongs to the realm of principle (*tattva*).

When the ultimate and conventional truths proceed together and principle and phenomena advance in tandem, then form and mind find their resting place, and the transformation of conditions proceeds without fail. Therefore, it is said that the meaning reaches its pinnacle here.
As for the citation in the text, the *sūtra* refers to the *Anuttarāśraya-sūtra*, as fully cited in the ninth chapter; it is also like the merit of creating an image.
The *Dejing* (Scripture on Virtue) states that there are eleven kinds of merit for creating images: first, one’s eyes shall be clear and pure in every lifetime;
second, one shall not encounter evil in the places where one is born; third, one shall always be born into a noble family; fourth, one’s body shall be like the color of purple-polished gold;

fifth, one shall abound in rare treasures and playthings; sixth, one shall be born into a family of the wise and virtuous; seventh, one shall be born to become a king; eighth, one shall... [text truncated]
[One becomes] a Golden Wheel-Turning King. Ninth, one is born in the Brahma Heaven with a lifespan of one kalpa. Tenth, one does not fall into the evil realms.

Eleventh, in future births, one is still able to revere and honor the Triple Gem. It is further said that if, at the moment of death, a person speaks the words to have an image made—even one as small as a grain of barley—it can eliminate the sins of birth and death accumulated over eight thousand billion kalpas throughout the three periods of time. Such a person is a vessel for the Dharma-body.

Because the Dharmakāya is all-pervasive, there is nowhere it does not abide. "Treatise" (*lun*) refers to wisdom (*jñāna*); it does not pertain to insentient matter or phenomenal events. "Manifestation" (*biaoxian*) pertains to principle (*li*).
Regarding the first section on the practice of ritual veneration: the first four lines arise from what precedes them. This means that even when an image is made of earth or stone, one venerates it.

If it is destroyed, sin and merit will accordingly arise. If there is an invocation for grace, one will naturally move the divine response. "Weeping" refers to the ultimate limit of sorrowful emotion.
However, the final two lines lament not beholding the manifested form (*nirmāṇakāya*). "Traces left behind" refers to the Three Jewels as maintained by the community.

The following four lines cite an analogy: "The Pure Temple" (*qīngmiào*) refers to the ancestral temple of the state. The commentary on the *Shijing* states: "The Pure Temple is for the sacrifice to [the ancestors]."
The palace of those of illustrious virtue refers to the ancestral temple (*miao*). It depicts the countenances of the ancestors so that they appear as if present.

This is what the *Analects* means when it says: "In sacrificing, as if [the ancestors] were present; in sacrificing to the spirits, as if the spirits were present. The following eight lines conform to this principle.

The first two lines state that the transformed manifestations have already passed away; only the final line states that the presiding master still remains. The subsequent section clarifies that the Buddha established these expedient means.
Therefore, one should practice accordingly. Now, the following provides a rebuttal. "The seer" refers to the sublime countenance above; "the hearer" refers to the sublime preaching above.
Regarding the phrase "because the mind lacks faith": the character *xin* (mind) is an error and should be read as *zhi* (to stop/cease); *zhi* here means "only. It may also be a scribal inversion.

When the character for "mind" (*xin*) is placed below [the character for "nature"], it signifies compliance. The first of the following two lines interrogates the reason for this; the subsequent two lines illustrate it by analogy.

This means that the three realms are created solely by the mind, and whatever one intends to employ is immediately accomplished. Thus, the *Yuanren lun* (Treatise on the Original Man) states: "The three poisons and three karmas of sentient beings create the vessel-world.

This is precisely what is meant. The final two lines provide a doctrinal explanation (*dharmadeśanā*). Regarding the term "obstinate ignorance" (*wanchi*), the old commentary interprets it as "troublesome ignorance" (*fanchi*).
This refers to the mind being deluded, afflicted, and ignorant. As for the phrase "the object remains unmoving," the original manuscript reads "obstinate and obstructive" (*wán'ài*).

The meaning is that although the vastness of the triple world is such that the mind might conceive it as smaller than a single hall, how could that which is composed of metal, stone, wood, and earth be considered "obstinate and obstructive" such that it cannot be moved or transformed?
Furthermore, one who is obstinate and ignorant calls upon those capable of reverence; this means that [one recognizes] one's own obstinacy and ignorance. It does not...
The Holy Countenance moved accordingly.

Regarding the "damage within the bonds," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* is identical to the *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. As it is said in the Sūtra: "I am obscured by the defilement of my turbid and evil eyes; thus I do not see you face-to-face."
Therefore, "not seeing," and so forth, refers to the lower [level], which means establishing [the practice] according to specific matters; all of these can be traced back to the mind.

"The Radiant Light" (*Prabhāsa*) verifies the former [point], as if facing a true image; "Expounding the Dharma" (*Dharmaparyāya*) verifies the latter, meaning "expounding the Dharma for me. "That which is required" (*apekṣita*): "required" (*xu*) is synonymous with "knowing" (*zhi*).
The following two phrases manifest the essential cultivation.

Regarding the section on "The Correct Clarification of Principle-Observation" (*lǐguān zhèngmíng*): This refers to reverently attending to the aforementioned objects. If one employs the illumination of wisdom (*zhìmíng*), all perceived forms (*rūpa*) are subsumed within principle-observation.

Because one sees that form is identical to mind and there is no phenomenon outside of mind, all sensory objects (*viṣaya*) are found to be unobtainable; this is the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).

Since true suchness (*tathatā*) has no substantial essence and all characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are empty, it is called "true observation" (*zhēnguān*). As for the statement that "in reality, only consciousness exists" (*shí wéi shí yǒu*): [this follows].
The contemplation thus cultivated is essentially the same as the preceding; however, because mental characteristics still persist, it is called "conventional contemplation" (*sāṃvṛta-vipaśyanā*).

This is similar to how other schools regard *tathatā* (suchness) as "contemplation of principle" (*li-guan*) and *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only) as "contemplation of phenomena" (*shi-guan*), since the latter is practiced by traversing through phenomena.
To speak in these terms, true contemplation belongs to principle and conventional contemplation pertains to phenomena. If one can contemplate both the true and the conventional simultaneously—
Thus, there is nothing that cannot be applied to the contemplation of principle. As the subsequent text states: "Knowing that objects have no existence, one penetrates True Suchness (tathatā);
realizing that there is only consciousness, one penetrates the conventional, and so forth."

The next section explains the superior cultivation of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) in the first four lines. Through the passage of years and days, each thought-moment becomes increasingly clear and each mind-state continues in succession;

by rehearsing it without forgetting, the wisdom of the mind becomes sharp and lucid, and one constantly dwells within it; therefore, it is said that "it increases further. The subsequent section distinguishes the entry into the stages (*bhūmi*).

Regarding the conditions of the provisional, such as sacred images and the like: these are established through provisional reliance. One knows them to be created solely by the mind; therefore, it is said "not [real]."

Delusion is dispelled through the cultivation of clarity, whereby one gradually enters the Noble Path. There are four stages for those who aspire to and delight in descending [from the higher realms]:

namely, the path of application (*prayoga-mārga*), the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*), the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), and the path beyond training (*aśaikṣa-mārga*). "Aspiring and delighting" refers to the path of application, which is also termed "expedient means" (*upāya*). According to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, this is the case.
This includes practitioners of the forty stages: the ten levels of faith (*śraddhā*), the ten abodes (*vihāra*), the ten practices (*caryā*), and the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*).

The path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) refers here to the second through the seventh stages (*bhūmi*). Although the text does not explicitly mention the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) and the path beyond training (*aśaikṣamārga*), it designates the preceding stage as "vision" (*darśana*).

The stage cultivated after this is called "no-more-learning" (*aśaikṣa*). To explain the etymology of the term "Śākyamuni": those who leave the household life to cultivate supramundane dharmas were originally called *dàorén* (persons of the Way) or *dàoshì* (masters of the Way).
Later, followers such as Li and Zhang usurped these titles; therefore, the Śākyas felt ashamed to share them and returned to using their original Indic name.
He then said, "O Bhikṣu. The term "practitioner" (xingzhe) likewise refers to one who practices the Way.
In the *Jiegao*, the first two lines constitute a self-description by one who has abandoned folly; they refer to those who are indolent and lack faith, who might resent such an address.
But would one refrain from speaking simply because of resentment? Therefore, he says, "It is truly a factual record. "Truly" (cheng) means genuine; "should" (dang) is equivalent to...
This is correct. The *Wei zhi* states that Wang Su remarked that Sima Qian’s recording of events was not false and that he did not conceal faults while praising virtues.
Liu Xiang and Yang Xiong admired his narrative style, asserting he possessed the talent of a true historian; they called it a "true record" (*shilu*) because it did not admit of flowery rhetoric.
From this point downward, [the text] encourages one to abandon folly and follow the Way. As Laozi said: "In practicing the Way, one diminishes day by day."
